## The One Formula

Everything in this chapter rests on a single rule for how a probability density
changes when you push it through an invertible map.  It relates the density in the
data world to the density in the simple (Gaussian) world through one correction
factor — the Jacobian determinant — and it is what lets us move between the two
worlds without losing or inventing any probability.

If $z = T(x)$ is an **invertible** map and $z$ has density $p_Z$, then $x$ has
density

$$
p_X(x) = p_Z\big(T(x)\big)\,\left|\det \frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right|.
$$

The Jacobian determinant is a *volume* correction: it accounts for how much $T$
stretches or squeezes space at $x$.  This single equation is the engine of the
course.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## What the Two Directions Mean

- **Forward** ($z = T(x)$, Gaussianize): the Jacobian tells you how much $T$ had
  to distort space to make $x$ look standard-normal — and that distortion *is* the
  dependence (made precise as [total correlation](03-mutual-information.qmd)).
- **Backward** ($x = T^{-1}(z)$): the formula is a sampling recipe — draw
  $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$ and apply $T^{-1}$ to get a sample of $x$.  This is
  the generative direction used in [Uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd).
:::

## Step 1: Uniformize — the Probability Integral Transform

Before we can make anything Gaussian, we need a universal way station that erases
every original shape.  That way station is the **uniform**, and the road to it is a
variable's *own* CDF.

Push **any** continuous variable $X$ through its own cumulative distribution
function $F_X$ and the result is flat — exactly $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, no matter
how skewed, fat-tailed, or oddly-shaped $X$ was to begin with:

$$
u = F_X(x) \ \sim\ \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1).
$$

This is the **Probability Integral Transform**.  The reason is almost a tautology:
$F_X(x)$ reads off *what fraction of the mass sits below $x$*, and "the fraction
below me" is uniform by construction — a quarter of the data lands below the 0.25
mark, half below the 0.5 mark, and so on.  Every feature of the original shape is
washed out; only the *ranking* survives.

```{python}
#| label: fig-uniformize-pit
#| fig-cap: "The Probability Integral Transform. A skewed exponential variable (left), read through its own empirical CDF (middle), comes out flat — a Uniform(0,1) (right). The shape is gone; only the ranking remains."
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
v = rng.exponential(size=4000)          # a skewed source variable
xs = np.sort(v)                          # sorted values define the empirical CDF
Fc = np.arange(1, len(xs) + 1) / len(xs) # F̂(x) = fraction of data at or below x
u = np.interp(v, xs, Fc)                 # u = F̂(x): each point's mass-fraction

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.4))
axes[0].hist(v, bins=40, color=WARM, alpha=0.85, density=True)
axes[0].set_title("data  x  (skewed)", fontsize=12)
axes[0].set_xlabel("x"); axes[0].set_ylabel("density")
axes[1].plot(xs, Fc, color=INK, lw=2.4)
axes[1].set_title(r"its CDF  $\hat F_X$  (a ruler in probability)", fontsize=12)
axes[1].set_xlabel("x"); axes[1].set_ylabel("cumulative fraction")
axes[2].hist(u, bins=20, color=COOL, alpha=0.85, density=True)
axes[2].axhline(1.0, color=INK, lw=1.6, ls="--", label="Uniform(0,1)")
axes[2].set_title(r"$u = \hat F_X(x)$  — flat", fontsize=12)
axes[2].set_xlabel("u"); axes[2].legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
for a in axes:
    despine(a)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The CDF is a **ruler measured in probability**.  Whatever the original units —
dollars, log-returns, waiting times — it relabels each point by the fraction of the
population beneath it, and that relabelling is always uniform.

## Step 2: Inverse CDF — a Uniform Becomes Anything

A uniform is not the destination; it is a hub.  Run the transform *backward* — feed
a uniform $u$ into some **target** distribution's inverse CDF $F^{-1}_{\text{target}}$
— and you arrive in *any* law you choose:

$$
z = F^{-1}_{\text{target}}(u).
$$

The same uniform draws can be sculpted into a Gaussian, a sharp-peaked Laplace, a
fat-tailed Student-$t$, or anything else with a CDF.  Uniform sits at the centre of
a wheel; each inverse CDF is a different spoke out.

```{python}
#| label: fig-inverse-cdf-anything
#| fig-cap: "One stream of uniform draws, pushed through three different inverse CDFs, lands in three different laws — Gaussian, Laplace (sharp peak), and Student-t with 3 degrees of freedom (fat tails)."
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
u = rng.uniform(size=9000)               # the universal hub: one uniform stream

targets = [
    ("Gaussian  ·  Φ⁻¹", norm.ppf(u), COOL),
    ("Laplace  ·  sharp peak", laplace.ppf(u), WARM),
    ("Student-t(3)  ·  fat tails", student_t(3).ppf(u), plotting.PALETTE["green"]),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.2))
for ax, (name, z, c) in zip(axes, targets):
    ax.hist(np.clip(z, -6, 6), bins=60, range=(-6, 6),
            color=c, alpha=0.85, density=True)  # clip only so the t-tails fit the frame
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xlim(-6, 6); ax.set_xlabel("z"); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

So the full menu is $x \to u \to \text{anything}$.  **Gaussianizing is simply
choosing the Gaussian exit** — $z = \Phi^{-1}(u)$ — out of all the spokes available.

## Step 3: Sampling for Free — Invert the CDF

Reading Step 2 as a recipe gives **inverse-transform sampling**, the cheapest
sampler there is.  To draw from *any* law: pick $u \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, ride
up to the CDF curve, and read off $z = F^{-1}(u)$.  No rejection, no MCMC — uniform
noise in, correctly-shaped samples out, with the curvature of the CDF doing all of
the bending.

This *is* the **backward / generative** pass of the change-of-variables formula:
draw simple noise in the easy world, invert the map to land in the data world.

```{python}
#| label: fig-inverse-transform-sampling
#| fig-cap: "Inverse-transform sampling. Uniform draws sit on the y-axis; each rides across to the CDF curve, then drops to a sample on the x-axis. Densely-sloped regions of the CDF catch more uniform draws, so samples pile up where the density is high."
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
zs = np.linspace(-3.4, 3.4, 400)
us = np.sort(rng.uniform(0.04, 0.96, size=9))   # nine uniform draws on the y-axis

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))
ax.plot(zs, norm.cdf(zs), color=INK, lw=2.4, label=r"CDF  $\Phi$")
for uu in us:
    zz = norm.ppf(uu)                            # z = Φ⁻¹(u): the sample for this draw
    ax.plot([-3.5, zz], [uu, uu], color=COOL, lw=1.0, alpha=0.8)  # ride across to the curve
    ax.plot([zz, zz], [uu, 0], color=WARM, lw=1.0, alpha=0.8)     # drop down to the x-axis
    ax.scatter([zz], [0], color=WARM, s=30, zorder=5)
ax.scatter([-3.5] * len(us), us, color=COOL, s=30, zorder=5)
ax.set_xlim(-3.6, 3.6); ax.set_ylim(-0.01, 1.02)
ax.set_xlabel(r"$z = \Phi^{-1}(u)$   →   Gaussian samples (x-axis)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$u \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$  (y-axis)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="lower right")
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Uniform draws are spread evenly up the y-axis, but the CDF is steep where the
density is high — so those flat draws get squeezed together near the mode and spread
out in the tails.  The shape of the samples is the shape of the inverse CDF.

## Step 4: The 1-D Gaussianization Move = Uniformize, then Exit Gaussian

Chaining the two halves gives the simplest non-trivial $T$: it makes a *single*
variable Gaussian.  Send each value through its own empirical CDF $\hat F_X$ (Step 1,
$x \to u$), then out through the inverse Gaussian CDF $\Phi^{-1}$ (the Gaussian
spoke of Step 2, $u \to z$):

$$
T(x) = \Phi^{-1}\big(\hat F_X(x)\big)\,,
\qquad
\underbrace{\hat F_X}_{x \,\to\, u}\ \text{then}\ \underbrace{\Phi^{-1}}_{u \,\to\, z}.
$$

Both pieces are monotone, so their composition is monotone — hence **invertible**,
exactly as the formula above requires.  It carries no information away; it only
*reshapes the marginal*.  Cross-dependence between variables is untouched (that is
what [rotation](02-rbig.qmd) is for).

```{python}
#| label: fig-gaussianize-1d
#| fig-cap: "A skewed (exponential) variable, before and after the rank → Gaussian transform T(x) = Φ⁻¹(F̂(x)). The shape becomes a standard normal; the ordering of points is preserved."
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
v = rng.exponential(size=4000)
g = gaussianize_1d(v)                     # T(x) = Φ⁻¹(F̂(x)): uniformize, then exit Gaussian

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))
axL.hist(v, bins=40, color=WARM, alpha=0.8, density=True)
axL.set_title("before:  heavy-skewed", fontsize=12)
axL.set_xlabel("x"); axL.set_ylabel("density")
despine(axL)

grid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 200)
axR.hist(g, bins=40, color=COOL, alpha=0.8, density=True)
axR.plot(grid, norm.pdf(grid), c=INK, lw=2, label="standard normal")
axR.set_title("after:  T(x) = Φ⁻¹(F̂(x))", fontsize=12)
axR.set_xlabel("z"); axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(axR)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

One marginal, now exactly standard normal — and because the map is monotone it is
invertible, so the next section's promise (a perfect dictionary back to the data)
still holds.

## Why Aim at a Gaussian?

Step 2 showed that *any* target is reachable — Laplace, Student-$t$, anything with a
CDF.  So why do we always aim at the bell?  Three reasons, and the second is the
hinge the whole iterative method (next note) turns on.

**(a) Maximum entropy for a fixed variance.**  Among all distributions with a given
variance, the Gaussian is the one with the largest entropy — the *least committal*,
most spread-out choice.  Picking it as the target adds no structure of our own
beyond the scale we fixed.

**(b) Rotation-invariance — the unique fixed point of a spin.**  A standard Gaussian
in $d$ dimensions is spherically symmetric: rotate it and it is unchanged.  Crucially,
it is the **only** shape for which independent coordinates *stay* independent under a
rotation.  Spin a cloud of independent Gaussians and you get independent Gaussians
again; spin a cloud of independent *uniforms* (or any non-Gaussian) and the axes
become dependent.  This is exactly the lever [RBIG](02-rbig.qmd) pulls: rotate, and
any leftover dependence is forced to *resurface as non-Gaussian marginals*, which the
1-D move can then flatten.

**(c) Closed form everywhere.**  Entropy, mutual information, and tail probabilities
of a Gaussian are all available in closed form, which is what makes the dependence
measures of [the next notes](03-mutual-information.qmd) computable rather than merely
defined.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rotation-invariance
#| fig-cap: "Why the Gaussian is special. Left: independent Gaussians, spun by 35°, are still independent Gaussians (round, axis-aligned marginals). Right: independent uniforms, spun by the same angle, become dependent — the square tilts into a diamond and the axes now carry information about each other."
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
G = rng.normal(size=(2500, 2))               # independent standard Gaussians
U = rng.uniform(-1.7, 1.7, size=(2500, 2))   # independent uniforms (matched spread)


def rotate(D, deg):
    """Rotate a 2-D point cloud by `deg` degrees."""
    th = np.deg2rad(deg)
    R = np.array([[np.cos(th), -np.sin(th)],
                  [np.sin(th),  np.cos(th)]])
    return D @ R.T


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.4, 4.0))
axes[0].scatter(*rotate(G, 35).T, s=5, c=COOL, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
axes[0].set_title("spin independent Gaussians\n→ still independent Gaussians", fontsize=11)
axes[1].scatter(*rotate(U, 35).T, s=5, c=WARM, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
axes[1].set_title("spin independent uniforms\n→ now dependent", fontsize=11)
for a in axes:
    a.set_aspect("equal"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([]); despine(a)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Reachability says we *could* aim anywhere; entropy, rotation-invariance, and
closed-form tractability say the Gaussian is where we *should*.

## Why Invertibility Is the Whole Point

A lossy transform (say, thresholding) cannot be undone, so you can never get back
to the data — no sampling, no exact likelihood.  An *invertible* $T$ keeps a
perfect dictionary between the two worlds.  Anything easy in Gaussian space
(independent coordinates, closed-form densities) can be pulled back to the data
exactly.

```{python}
#| label: fig-monotone-map
#| fig-cap: "The 1-D map is monotone: it relabels the axis without reordering points, so it is exactly invertible."
order = np.argsort(v)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
ax.plot(v[order], g[order], c=COOL, lw=2.5)
ax.set_xlabel("x  (data value)"); ax.set_ylabel("z = T(x)  (Gaussian value)")
ax.set_title("A monotone, invertible relabelling", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(ax, 0.5, -0.12, "rank preserved  ⇒  no information lost")
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.eli5}
**One-liner.**  Change of variables is a currency exchange between probability
worlds; the Jacobian is the exchange rate.  Make the rate invertible and you can
always convert back.
:::

Next: stack this 1-D move with rotations to Gaussianize the *joint* — [RBIG](02-rbig.qmd).
